summary:
Niger criminalises same-sex conduct and transition itself. Article 25 of the Charte de la Refondation, adopted by the military government in March 2025, bans "LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior" for the five-year transition that followed the July 2023 coup. It was the first explicit statutory prohibition of the conduct in the country and it set no penalty of its own. The February 2026 revision of the penal code supplies the penalties; the Agence Nigérienne de Presse reported the criminalisation of LGBTQIA+ practice on 1 June 2026.

Article 390 punishes "indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts" with five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs. The article reaches the public announcement of a same-sex relationship and anyone who changes or attempts to change their sex at birth, which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside the criminal law. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are unavailable under the article.

Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years' imprisonment. Article 392 punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs, about US$882,829.

The drafting reaches further than its headings suggest. El Espectador reported on 29 July 2026 that the code's broad and confused wording reads asexuality as sanctionable conduct. The Oxford Human Rights Hub stated in July 2026 that the ban in Article 390 on artificially changing sex at birth violates the human rights of intersex people as well as LGBTQIA+ people.

Enforcement since the code took effect has been documented as a coordinated campaign. The Guardian reported on 1 July 2026 that at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned, with campaigners describing a witch-hunt in a toxic climate. Local media reported dozens of arrests across the country, some of those detained being military officials. These are raw counts reported without a population denominator, so they show the scale of the crackdown rather than per-capita risk. LGBTQ people went into hiding after the law; before it, many had led publicly acceptable lives while keeping relationships private.

Prosecution of women over alleged same-sex conduct predates the 2026 code. In Maradi in 2022 two young women were prosecuted over lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then criminalised it, but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under Article 276 on public indecency, which carried up to three years, and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In Niamey in 2025 two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was allegedly sanctioned for excessive leniency. In December 2022 lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women because no legislation existed.

Access to HIV prevention has collapsed for the population those services targeted. After the 2026 law, organisations providing HIV prevention to men who have sex with men stopped working, and a representative warned that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP. The Guardian reported fears of an HIV resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses. Two gay rights organisations had operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered.

Niger has no broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 95 of the 2022 law on the protection of personal data prohibits collecting or processing data revealing sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; the law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025. The only other statutory protection, in Article 4 of the 2015 law on illicit trafficking of migrants, was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Officials have framed the measures in cultural terms. Justice Minister Alio Daouda said that "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be" are "not in line with our social and cultural values". Public discourse under President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals centred on "social contagion".

Asylum seekers who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022, from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, faced societal discrimination including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers, and the authorities refused to recognise their refugee status.
tangentialFactors:
El Espectador placed the February 2026 code in a wider pattern on 29 July 2026, describing a wave of African states hardening laws against LGBTQIA+ people. The comparison is directional rather than measured; the source offers no ranking or penalty-by-penalty comparison between the states concerned.

The 2023 draft penal code proposed lighter and differently shaped penalties than the enacted text: up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing homosexual organisations. The February 2026 code as reported sets ten to twenty years for organisations and ten to twenty years for same-sex marriage, so the draft figures should not be read as the current rule.

Under the rules in force before March 2025 the age of consent was unequal, at 13 for different-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts. The age of consent set by the February 2026 code is not stated in this record.

The U.S. State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report recorded no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, while cautioning that stigma or intimidation probably kept incidents unreported; the same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested and fined for public indecency. That is a 2013 snapshot and does not describe the period under the 2026 code.

Stigmatisation of LGBTQIA+ people among the broader population is recorded as a standing condition of Nigerian society, and it is the mechanism the sources give for underreporting of both violence and discrimination.
localsOnly:
Organisations serving LGBTQIA+ people cannot operate after the 2026 code. Article 392 reaches creating, managing, financing or participating in such organisations, clubs and social venues directly or indirectly, and organisations providing HIV prevention to men who have sex with men stopped working, cutting off condoms, HIV testing and PrEP for their clients. Two gay rights organisations had previously run in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Article 95 of the 2022 personal data protection law bars the collection or processing of data revealing sexual orientation, with three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs. The law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025.

Judicial officers have faced consequences for outcomes in these cases. The judge who acquitted two women charged with same-sex intimacy in 2023 was reassigned to an administrative post, and the judge who acquitted two women in Niamey in 2025 was allegedly sanctioned for excessive leniency.

Niger's authorities refused to recognise the refugee status of the asylum seekers, from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, who staged the country's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022. Those protesters faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers.

Since the 2026 law, LGBTQ people have gone into hiding. Before it, many had led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private, and the record documents no broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity for residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 25 of the Charte de la Refondation remains in force alongside the February 2026 penal code, and whether draft provisions not carried into the enacted text survive, is unresolved in this record.

No source in this inventory addresses gender markers on passports, visa or entry screening, or document inspection for trans visitors. Nothing should be inferred either way from their absence.

The record contains no trans-specific violence or killing figure for Niger with a population denominator, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made here.

The figure of at least 40 arrests reported on 1 July 2026 is attributed to reporting and campaigner accounts rather than an official tally, and no later total is sourced. Whether the 16 imprisonments include convictions or pre-trial detention is not stated.

The age of consent under the February 2026 code, and whether the pre-2025 disparity of 13 versus 21 was retained, is not sourced. Enforcement of Article 95 of the data protection law is likewise undocumented in this inventory.
